title: Throughput harness: execution playbook and triage checklist
content:
Purpose
This doc is an operational playbook for running throughput experiments against the serving runtime and for triaging when runs disagree with historical baselines. It collects practical heuristics we use during day-to-day investigations: load generator configs, adaptive warmup rules, artifact collection checklist, and a fast triage flow for noisy runs.

Why this exists (short)
- We want runs that are reproducible and actionable (not just a single flaky numbers dump).
- Provide a consistent set of artifacts so root cause analysis (RCA) doesn’t stall.
- Capture ad-hoc heuristics we repeatedly use so new engineers can onboard faster.

Quick summary (TL;DR)
- Always run baseline + candidate in the same environment back-to-back.
- Use adaptive warmup: run until metric drift < 2% for 3 consecutive windows or max warmup time 8 min.
- Collect: nvprof/nsys trace, system metrics (node_exporter + dcgm), model server logs (TRACE), process-level perf sampling, and a snapshot of active containers + GPUs.
- If p95/p99 deviates >5% vs baseline, escalate to "stability triage" and attach all artifacts.

Run types (examples)
- Microbench: single connection, synthetic tokens (short sequence), measure per-step kernel timings.
- Steady-state throughput: N concurrent streams at target qps, realistic prompt length distribution.
- Burst profile: short high-QPS bursts to exercise autoscaling/fallback.
- Cold-start profile: measure latency and load while nodes are spinning up.

Load generator config templates (conceptual fields)
- client_concurrency: int (number of async streams)
- target_qps: float (requests/sec)
- max_tokens: int
- seq_length_dist: path/to/seq-dist.json (histogram or list)
- input_corpus: path/to/prompts.txt
- request_rate_mode: steady | poisson | burst
- measurement_window: 30s (default); shorter windows for microbench

Sample command (bench-runner shim)
- bench-runner run --scenario steady-state --concurrency 128 --qps 800 --seq-dist configs/short-medium.json --warmup-policy adaptive --results-dir /tmp/run123

Warmup heuristics (adaptive warmup algorithm)
- Rationale: fixed warmup time often over/under estimates. Adaptive warms until internal caches, batch sizes, and schedulers stabilize.
- Algorithm (operational description):
  1) Start load at 25% target_qps for 60s to allow initial JVM/Python imports and shared-memory set-up.
  2) Ramp linearly to target_qps over 120s.
  3) After reaching target, sample throughput and p95 every 30s.
  4) Compute relative change between consecutive windows: delta = abs(curr - prev)/prev.
  5) If delta for throughput and p95 < 0.02 (2%) for 3 consecutive windows -> warmup complete.
  6) Stop warmup when total warmup time > 480s (8 min) regardless.
- Notes: for small models (<7B) reduce ramp to 60s; for large models (>70B) allow slower ramp and increase sample window to 60s.

Repeatability checklist (before you start)
- Node images and driver versions pinned in the run metadata.
- No other workloads on test machines (confirmed via `htop` and `nvidia-smi -l 1` during run).
- CPU governor set to performance.
- Power limit configured consistently (record using `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=power.limit`).
- Model binary/checkpoint sha logged.
- Bench-runner commit hash recorded.
- Empty caches: Decide whether you are testing with warm caches or after clearing pagecache/kvcache. Document choice.

Mandatory artifacts to collect (minimum)
- bench-runner raw CSV (per-request latencies, timestamps)
- aggregated summary JSON (p50/p90/p95/p99, tokens/sec, error rate)
- nsys / perf trace covering the interesting window (attach compressed).
- Node-level metrics (node_exporter, dcgm) covering 5m before -> 5m after case.
- `docker ps -a` / `kubectl get pods -o wide` snapshot.
- Model server logs (INFO/ERROR/TRACE) for run time range.
- Environment snapshot: kernel, driver, CUDA, cuDNN, python runtime, package list (pip freeze).
- A short writeup (2–4 bullets) describing what was being measured and why.

Profiling hooks and where to use them
- Lightweight first pass: collect DCGM + node_exporter + bench CSV. If behavior is within noise, stop.
- If headroom or tail latency anomaly: collect Nsight Systems (nsys) for 30–120s around anomaly, with context switch and CPU sampling enabled.
- Kernel-level hotpaths: use `nvprof`/`nvdisasm` or CUPTI sampling (note: nvprof deprecated, use Nsight or CUPTI).
- CPU-side hotspots: perf record -F 99 -g --call-graph dwarf -p <pid>.
- TensorLib counters: enable library-specific counters when model kernels are suspect (e.g., cuBLAS flops if throughput low).

Common failure modes and quick checks
- High p99 with normal p50/p95: look for rare backpressure events – check request queues length and scheduler logs.
- Low throughput but high GPU utilization: likely memory bandwidth or kernel inefficiency; collect nsys to inspect kernel durations and occupancy.
- Low throughput and low GPU utilization: batching/queueing misconfiguration or network bottleneck. Check grpc queue wait times and host CPU saturation.
- Run-to-run variance: check for background cron jobs, warped power limits, or dynamic frequency scaling.

Triage flow (fast)
1) Reproduce: re-run baseline config vs candidate back-to-back with the exact same node image. If not reproducible -> flakiness.
2) If reproducible and regression persists -> run nsys for 60–120s on both runs.
3) Compare kernel timelines (nsys) and perf: look for additional long kernels or increased kernel counts.
4) Check scheduler metrics: look for queueing spikes or dropped requests.
5) If still unclear, escalate to eng-serving-runtime with artifacts and a 5-bullet summary.

Experiment naming and metadata (small checklist)
- name: team-scenario-model-variant-20251103-01 (date + sequence)
- bench-runner_sha: git hash
- node_image: ami-... or gke node tag
- driver_cuda: driver: 535.86 / cuda: 12.1 (example)
- model_sha: git+sha or checkpoint id

Notes-to-self / gotchas
- Don’t trust a single warmup run. At minimum 3 independent repeat runs for the same config (sequentially) and report median.
- Small differences in network MTU or container cgroup CPU shares can create 5–10% noise. Record them.
- When comparing quantized vs fp16 kernels, also collect model output correctness (token-level diffs) to ensure we're not trading away quality.

Example short RCA (template)
- Symptom: p95 increased from 220ms -> 310ms on candidate (20% regression)
- Repro: reproduced on two runs (medians: baseline 225ms, candidate 308ms)
- Key artifacts: bench CSV, nsys trace, node metrics, model server logs.
- Root cause: discovered a new memory fence inserted in scheduler when using dynamic batch sizing, causing synchronous flushes at 1/30s intervals.
- Fix: revert dynamic-batching flag and re-run – p95 back to 228ms.

Open questions / possible future improvements
- Auto-annotate traces with request ids so we can correlate a specific slow request to trace spans.
- Integrate bench-runner with the console so each run auto-upload artifacts to costed S3 and attaches a link to the run metadata.
- Better machine learning model to predict stabilization time from warmup traces so we can avoid fixed timeouts.

References and useful commands
- nsys example: nsys profile --trace=cuda,osrt --output /tmp/nsys_run --capture-range=nvtx --force-overwrite --capture-start=immediate --duration 120s -- <server command>
- perf: sudo perf record -F 99 -g -p <pid> -o perf.data -- sleep 30 && perf report -i perf.data
- dcgm metrics collection: dcgmi dmon -e -d 1 --output /tmp/dcgmi.csv

Appendix: quick-check checklist (copyable)
- [ ] bench-runner sha recorded
- [ ] model sha/checkpoint recorded
- [ ] drivers and cuda versions recorded
- [ ] nodes idle/confirmed
- [ ] run CSV + summary JSON captured
- [ ] nsys/perf trace attached (if anomaly)
- [ ] node metrics (dcgm / node_exporter) preserved

If you use this doc, please add a 2-line summary at the top of the results directory describing what went well/what didn’t, and add tags for easy search (e.g., "stable-runs", "regressed-dynbatch").

-- end --
